title: Chapter XI

teacherSummary.text: Elizabeth and Darcy discuss faults: he admits to a resentful temper—'my good opinion once lost is lost forever'—while she teases that his flaw is to hate everybody.

vocabulary.definition: In a manner or to a degree beyond endurance
vocabulary.context: “I should like balls infinitely better,” she replied, “if they were carried on in a different manner; but there is something insufferably tedious in the usual process of such a meeting.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “insufferably”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + fer (Latin ferre, "to carry, bear") + -ly (Old English -lice, "in the manner of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To defeat of expectation or hope
vocabulary.context: “Not at all,” was her answer; “but depend upon it, he means to be severe on us, and our surest way of disappointing him, will be to ask nothing about it.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “disappoint”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To persist in any business or enterprise undertaken
vocabulary.context: Darcy in anything, and persevered therefore in requiring an explanation of his two motives.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “persevere”: per- (Latin per, "through, thoroughly"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: An ornamental band or ring, for the wrist or the arm
vocabulary.context: Hurst, principally occupied in playing with her bracelets and rings, joined now and then in her brother’s conversation with Miss Bennet.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “bracelet”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being weak
vocabulary.context: But it has been the study of my life to avoid those weaknesses which often expose a strong understanding to ridicule.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “weakness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Her figure was elegant, and she walked well;—but Darcy, at whom it was all aimed, was still inflexibly studious.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “studious”: -ious (Latin -iosus, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To bring together, literally or figuratively
vocabulary.context: He was directly invited to join their party, but he declined it, observing that he could imagine but two motives for their choosing to walk up and down the room together, with either of which motives his joining them would interfere.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “join”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: “If you mean Darcy,” cried her brother, “he may go to bed, if he chooses, before it begins—but as for the ball, it is quite a settled thing; and as soon as Nicholls has made white soup enough I shall send round my cards.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “choose”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: The state of quality of being calm
vocabulary.context: Tease calmness of temper and presence of mind!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “calmness”: -ness (Old English -ness, "state of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The part a chimney appropriated to the fire
vocabulary.context: The first half hour was spent in piling up the fire, lest she should suffer from the change of room; and she removed at his desire to the other side of the fireplace, that she might be farther from the door.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “fireplace”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

context.history: Self-examination was a common moral exercise in conduct literature.

significance: Darcy names his pride directly; the novel will test whether either can change.
discussionQuestions: Darcy says his good opinion once lost is lost forever. Is this pride or integrity?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with first impressions and prejudice?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XI,” how does Austen show character flaws examined? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XI, how does Austen develop the idea of character flaws examined? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XI develops the idea of character flaws examined. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XI (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of character flaws examined. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XI suggests about character flaws examined. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and theme), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XI to complicate the reader's understanding of character flaws examined. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XI within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of character flaws examined responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XI alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of character flaws examined follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XI and its treatment of character flaws examined. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and theme, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XI as evidence for a larger claim about character flaws examined in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XI as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of character flaws examined. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.passage: But when the gentlemen entered, Jane was no longer the first object. Miss Bingley’s eyes were instantly turned towards Darcy, and she had something to say to him before he had advanced many steps. He addressed himself directly to Miss Bennet, with a polite congratulation; Mr. Hurst also made her a slight bow, and said he was “very glad;” but diffuseness and warmth remained for Bingley’s salutation. He was full of joy and attention. The first half hour was spent in piling up the fire, lest she should suffer from the change of room; and she removed at his desire to the other side of the fireplace, that she might be farther from the door. He then sat down by her, and talked scarcely to anyone else. Elizabeth, at work in the opposite corner, saw it all with great delight.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XI”?

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Darcy says his good opinion once lost is lost forever. Is this pride or integrity? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are insufferably, disappointing, persevered, bracelets, weaknesses. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: ““I should like balls infinitely better,” she replied, “if they were carried on in a different manner; but there is something insufferably tedious in the usual process of such a meeting.” Webster's says: In a manner or to a degree beyond endurance. Now the word history: “insufferably”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + fer (Latin ferre, "to carry, bear") + -ly (Old English -lice, "in the manner of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “disappoint”: dis- (Latin dis-, "apart, not"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “persevere”: per- (Latin per, "through, thoroughly"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Self-examination was a common moral exercise in conduct literature. Why does this chapter matter? Darcy names his pride directly; the novel will test whether either can change. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to character flaws examined.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Theme, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
